name: 100% stacked bar (relative composition)
reader_question: How does the mix of a measure differ across groups, and how large is each group's base?
relationship: Part-to-whole as shares: each row sums to 100% of its own base, shown beside the bar.
use_when: The mix matters more than the absolute total
Row bases differ and the reader needs to see by how much
avoid_when: Absolute size is the point — use stacked-bar
Row shares do not sum to 100 and cannot be derived from counts

data_contract.notes: Share unit and what each base n counts
Shares must sum to 100 per row; counts are converted to shares and the derivation is stated on the slide
Stacking order and at most one highlighted component
n is required for shares and derived for counts

units: Per cent of each row's own base; the axis is fixed at 0–100% and hidden.

editable: 100% stacked bar chart with embedded workbook (Edit Data)
not_data_bound: Row bases (n) and the basis note are positioned text computed from the fixture
Labels below 7% are hidden by a number-format condition, not deleted

table_alternative: A table of counts and shares per row with the base in its own column.
variations: Counts input with shares derived on the slide
limitations: Shares from small bases are volatile; the base is shown but not a confidence interval
Equal bar lengths can read as equal totals

excluded_alternatives.reason: Many slices and no common baseline make cross-group comparison unreliable
Unequal totals hide the difference in mix; see stacked-bar when size matters
